claim: Peripheral nerve injury-induced neuropathic pain is a chronic and debilitating condition characterized by mechanical hypersensitivity.
source: Peripheral nerve injury-induced neuropathic pain is a chronic and debilitating condition characterized by mechanical hypersensitivity.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about neuropathic pain characteristics.

claim: Intrathecal administration of CSF1, even in the absence of injury, is sufficient to induce pain behavior in male mice but not in female mice.
source: Here, we show that intrathecal administration of CSF1, even in the absence of injury, is sufficient to induce pain behavior, but only in male mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript, specifically behavioral testing results.

claim: Intrathecal CSF1 induces robust immune activation in male but not female microglia.
source: Transcriptional profiling and morphologic analyses after intrathecal CSF1 showed robust immune activation in male but not female microglia.
evidence: This claim is supported by transcriptional profiling data and morphological analyses presented in the manuscript.

claim: CSF1 induces marked expansion of lymphocytes within the spinal cord meninges.
source: CSF1 also induced marked expansion of lymphocytes within the spinal cord meninges, with preferential expansion of regulatory T-cells (Tregs) in female mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data of meningeal immune cells.

claim: CSF1 induces preferential expansion of regulatory T-cells (Tregs) in female mice compared to male mice.
source: CSF1 also induced marked expansion of lymphocytes within the spinal cord meninges, with preferential expansion of regulatory T-cells (Tregs) in female mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data showing differential Treg expansion between sexes.

claim: Treg deficient (Foxp3DTR) female mice show increased CSF1-induced microglial activation equivalent to males.
source: Consistent with the hypothesis that Tregs actively suppress microglial activation in females, Treg deficient (Foxp3DTR) female mice showed increased CSF1-induced microglial activation and pain hypersensitivity equivalent to males.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from Treg-depleted mice showing increased microglial activation.

claim: Treg deficient (Foxp3DTR) female mice show increased CSF1-induced pain hypersensitivity equivalent to males.
source: Consistent with the hypothesis that Tregs actively suppress microglial activation in females, Treg deficient (Foxp3DTR) female mice showed increased CSF1-induced microglial activation and pain hypersensitivity equivalent to males.
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral testing data from Treg-depleted female mice.

claim: Sexual dimorphism in the contribution of microglia to pain results from Treg-mediated suppression of microglial activation and pain hypersensitivity in female mice.
source: We conclude that sexual dimorphism in the contribution of microglia to pain results from Treg-mediated suppression of microglial activation and pain hypersensitivity in female mice.
evidence: This is the main conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Microglia are brain resident macrophages with essential roles in neural circuit function in physiology and disease.
source: Microglia are brain resident macrophages with essential roles in neural circuit function in physiology and disease (Priller and Prinz, 2019; Hammond et al., 2018; Vainchtein and Molofsky, 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to established literature on microglia.

claim: Microglia respond in sexually dimorphic ways in a variety of contexts, including autism, stroke, neurodegenerative diseases, and pain processing.
source: Microglia respond in sexually dimorphic ways in a variety of contexts, including autism, stroke, neurodegenerative diseases, and interestingly in the microglial contribution to pain processing (Mogil, 2020; Villa et al., 2018; Weinhard et al., 2018; Sorge et al., 2011; Inyang et al., 2019; Rosen et al., 2019; Kodama and Gan, 2019; Guneykaya et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to published literature.

claim: Male and female microglia are competent to induce pain.
source: For example, although male and female microglia are competent to induce pain (Yi et al., 2021), pharmacologic ablation or chemogenetic inhibition of microglia reverses peripheral nerve injury-induced mechanical hypersensitivity only in male mice (Sorge et al., 2015; Saika et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Yi et al., 2021.

claim: Pharmacologic ablation or chemogenetic inhibition of microglia reverses peripheral nerve injury-induced mechanical hypersensitivity only in male mice.
source: For example, although male and female microglia are competent to induce pain (Yi et al., 2021), pharmacologic ablation or chemogenetic inhibition of microglia reverses peripheral nerve injury-induced mechanical hypersensitivity only in male mice (Sorge et al., 2015; Saika et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Sorge et al., 2015 and Saika et al., 2020.

claim: Inhibition of microglia is sufficient to reverse injury-induced hypersensitivity in B- and T-cell deficient female mice.
source: In contrast, inhibition of microglia is sufficient to reverse injury-induced hypersensitivity in B- and T-cell deficient female mice (Sorge et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Sorge et al., 2015.

claim: There are sex-specific differences in how the innate and adaptive immune compartments interact to regulate neuropathic pain.
source: Taken together, these data imply that there are sex-specific differences in how the innate and adaptive immune compartments interact to regulate neuropathic pain.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the cited literature on sex differences in microglial contributions to pain.

claim: Female AvilCre:Csf1fl/fl mice (Adv-CSF1) developed normal mechanical hypersensitivity after peripheral nerve injury.
source: We found that female Adv-CSF1 mice developed normal mechanical hypersensitivity after peripheral nerve injury (Figure 1—figure supplement Figure 1—figure supplement 1A, B), in contrast to male rats and mice, in which hypersensitivity was CSF1-dependent (Guan et al., 2016; Okubo et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A, B.

claim: In male rats and mice, nerve injury-induced hypersensitivity is CSF1-dependent.
source: We found that female Adv-CSF1 mice developed normal mechanical hypersensitivity after peripheral nerve injury (Figure 1—figure supplement Figure 1—figure supplement 1A, B), in contrast to male rats and mice, in which hypersensitivity was CSF1-dependent (Guan et al., 2016; Okubo et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Guan et al., 2016 and Okubo et al., 2016.

claim: CSF1 is not required to induce mechanical hypersensitivity in female mice.
source: Thus, CSF1 is not required to induce mechanical hypersensitivity in females.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the experimental data showing normal hypersensitivity in CSF1-deficient female mice after nerve injury.

claim: Three consecutive injections of CSF1 provoked profound mechanical hypersensitivity in male mice.
source: Three consecutive injections of CSF1 provoked profound mechanical hypersensitivity in male, but not in female mice (Figure 1A–C), even at very high doses (30 ng; Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 1A-C.

claim: Three consecutive injections of CSF1 did not provoke mechanical hypersensitivity in female mice, even at very high doses (30 ng).
source: Three consecutive injections of CSF1 provoked profound mechanical hypersensitivity in male, but not in female mice (Figure 1A–C), even at very high doses (30 ng; Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 1A-C and Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: After intrathecal CSF1, male microglia acquired a robust amoeboid morphology, characterized by loss of ramification.
source: Furthermore, after intrathecal CSF1, male microglia acquired a robust amoeboid morphology, characterized by loss of ramification, but in females, microglia acquired a highly ramified morphology, consistent with a persistent homeostatic phenotype (Figure 1D–E).
evidence: This claim is supported by morphological analysis data shown in Figure 1D-E.

claim: After intrathecal CSF1, female microglia acquired a highly ramified morphology, consistent with a persistent homeostatic phenotype.
source: Furthermore, after intrathecal CSF1, male microglia acquired a robust amoeboid morphology, characterized by loss of ramification, but in females, microglia acquired a highly ramified morphology, consistent with a persistent homeostatic phenotype (Figure 1D–E).
evidence: This claim is supported by morphological analysis data shown in Figure 1D-E.

claim: FACS analysis revealed larger numbers of microglia in males after CSF1 treatment.
source: Fluorescence-activated cell sorting (FACS) analysis also revealed larger numbers of microglia in males and higher expression of cell surface activation markers, CD11b/CD45 (Figure 1F–H, Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by FACS data shown in Figure 1F-H.

claim: FACS analysis revealed higher expression of cell surface activation markers, CD11b/CD45, in male microglia after CSF1 treatment.
source: Fluorescence-activated cell sorting (FACS) analysis also revealed larger numbers of microglia in males and higher expression of cell surface activation markers, CD11b/CD45 (Figure 1F–H, Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by FACS data shown in Figure 1F-H and Figure 1—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Intrathecal CSF1 demonstrates a male-specific impact and sufficiency for microglia activation and pain hypersensitivity.
source: Taken together, these data demonstrate a male-specific impact and sufficiency of CSF1 for microglia activation and pain hypersensitivity.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion drawn from the behavioral, morphological, and FACS data presented.

claim: Sex differences in microglia gene expression were modest at baseline (86 genes, pAdj<0.01).
source: Sex differences were modest at baseline (86 genes, pAdj<0.01), and CSF1 induced robust gene expression changes in both male and female microglia (Figure 2A, PC1, 56% of variance).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA sequencing data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: CSF1 induced robust gene expression changes in both male and female microglia, accounting for 56% of variance in PC1.
source: Sex differences were modest at baseline (86 genes, pAdj<0.01), and CSF1 induced robust gene expression changes in both male and female microglia (Figure 2A, PC1, 56% of variance).
evidence: This claim is supported by principal component analysis of RNA sequencing data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: CSF1 induced an 8.3-fold increase in differentially expressed genes (both upregulated and downregulated) in male microglia compared to female microglia.
source: However, CSF1 induced an 8.3-fold increase in differentially expressed genes (both upregulated and downregulated) in male microglia (Figure 2B, Supplementary file 1; adjusted p-value<0.01: males 1350 genes, females 165 genes).
evidence: This claim is supported by differential gene expression analysis shown in Figure 2B.

claim: CSF1 treatment resulted in 1350 differentially expressed genes in male microglia (adjusted p-value<0.01).
source: However, CSF1 induced an 8.3-fold increase in differentially expressed genes (both upregulated and downregulated) in male microglia (Figure 2B, Supplementary file 1; adjusted p-value<0.01: males 1350 genes, females 165 genes).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA sequencing data analysis shown in Figure 2B.

claim: CSF1 treatment resulted in 165 differentially expressed genes in female microglia (adjusted p-value<0.01).
source: However, CSF1 induced an 8.3-fold increase in differentially expressed genes (both upregulated and downregulated) in male microglia (Figure 2B, Supplementary file 1; adjusted p-value<0.01: males 1350 genes, females 165 genes).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA sequencing data analysis shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Neither the protein nor transcriptomic CSF1R levels differed between males and females.
source: Neither the protein nor transcriptomic CSF1R levels differed between males and females (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A, B).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry and RNA sequencing data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A, B.

claim: Both male and female microglia responded to CSF1 with a decrease in homeostatic gene expression and an increase in proliferative genes, which were more prominent in males than females.
source: Both male and female microglia responded to CSF1 with a decrease in homeostatic gene expression and an increase in proliferative genes, which were more prominent in males than females.
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of gene expression changes in the context of published microglial transcriptomic datasets.

claim: Male microglia showed a striking upregulation of pathology-associated microglial activation genes (Neurodegeneration module) after CSF1 treatment.
source: Most prominent in male microglia was a striking upregulation of pathology-associated microglial activation genes (Figure 2C; Neurodegeneration module) (Friedman et al., 2018; Keren-Shaul et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by gene expression analysis shown in Figure 2C and comparison with published modules from Friedman et al., 2018.

claim: Male microglia induced genes and GO terms linked to classical immune activation and recruitment pathways after CSF1 treatment.
source: Gene ontology (GO) enrichment analysis (Figure 2D) revealed that male microglia induced genes and GO terms that are linked to classical immune activation and recruitment pathways, including many (Itgax, Lpl, Ccl3, Cybb, Clec7a, and Ctsb) associated with the 'disease associated microglia' DAM phenotype identified in single-cell sequencing experiments (Butovsky and Weiner, 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by gene ontology analysis shown in Figure 2D and citation to Butovsky and Weiner, 2018.

claim: Genes Itgax, Lpl, Ccl3, Cybb, Clec7a, and Ctsb are associated with the 'disease associated microglia' (DAM) phenotype.
source: Gene ontology (GO) enrichment analysis (Figure 2D) revealed that male microglia induced genes and GO terms that are linked to classical immune activation and recruitment pathways, including many (Itgax, Lpl, Ccl3, Cybb, Clec7a, and Ctsb) associated with the 'disease associated microglia' DAM phenotype identified in single-cell sequencing experiments (Butovsky and Weiner, 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Butovsky and Weiner, 2018.

claim: Ctsb has been linked to chronic pain.
source: Some of these genes, for example, Ctsb, have been linked to chronic pain (Sun et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Sun et al., 2012.

claim: Male microglia downregulated genes facilitating responsiveness to extracellular signals and some supportive functions, such as extracellular matrix regulation, after CSF1 treatment.
source: In addition, male microglia downregulated genes facilitating responsiveness to extracellular signals as well as some supportive functions, for example, extracellular matrix regulation (Figure 2D).
evidence: This claim is supported by gene ontology analysis shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Intrathecal CSF1 triggers pain hypersensitivity in male mice and induces robust transcriptomic changes associated with inflammatory activation in male but not female microglia.
source: Taken together, intrathecal CSF1 not only triggers pain hypersensitivity in male mice, but also induces robust transcriptomic changes associated with inflammatory activation in male but not female microglia.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion drawn from the behavioral and transcriptomic data presented.

claim: Other immune cells contribute to amplify or suppress the microglial response to CSF1.
source: Our findings suggest that other immune cells contribute to amplify or suppress the microglial response to CSF1.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the sex-specific differences in microglial responses to CSF1.

claim: The CNS meninges have a rich population of immune cells that mirrors the composition of tissue resident immune cells in other organs.
source: The CNS meninges have a rich population of immune cells that mirrors the composition of tissue resident immune cells in other organs (Alves de Lima et al., 2020; Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Alves de Lima et al., 2020 and flow cytometry data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Meningeal lymphocyte-derived cytokines impact CNS function in both normal and pathologic settings.
source: Meningeal lymphocyte-derived cytokines also impact CNS function in both normal and pathologic settings (Liu et al., 2020; Pasciuto et al., 2020; Ribeiro et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Liu et al., 2020, Pasciuto et al., 2020, and Ribeiro et al., 2019.

claim: Intrathecal CSF1 expanded meningeal macrophages.
source: As expected, intrathecal CSF1 expanded meningeal macrophages (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B), but we also observed a marked increase in lymphocytes, 6.5-fold in males and 9-fold in females (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Intrathecal CSF1 resulted in a marked increase in meningeal lymphocytes, 6.5-fold in males and 9-fold in females.
source: As expected, intrathecal CSF1 expanded meningeal macrophages (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B), but we also observed a marked increase in lymphocytes, 6.5-fold in males and 9-fold in females (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: CSF1 treatment resulted in a similar increase of CD4+ FoxP3- T cells, CD8+ T cells, B cells, and ILC2 cells in male and female meninges.
source: Further examination of lymphocyte subsets demonstrated a similar increase of CD4+ FoxP3 T cells, CD8+ T cells, B cells, and ILC2 cells in male and female meninges, but also revealed a significantly greater expansion of regulatory T cells and natural killer (NK) cells in female mice (Figure 3B–C).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 3B-C.

claim: CSF1 treatment resulted in a significantly greater expansion of regulatory T cells in female mice compared to male mice.
source: Further examination of lymphocyte subsets demonstrated a similar increase of CD4+ FoxP3 T cells, CD8+ T cells, B cells, and ILC2 cells in male and female meninges, but also revealed a significantly greater expansion of regulatory T cells and natural killer (NK) cells in female mice (Figure 3B–C).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 3B-C.

claim: CSF1 treatment resulted in a significantly greater expansion of natural killer (NK) cells in female mice compared to male mice.
source: Further examination of lymphocyte subsets demonstrated a similar increase of CD4+ FoxP3 T cells, CD8+ T cells, B cells, and ILC2 cells in male and female meninges, but also revealed a significantly greater expansion of regulatory T cells and natural killer (NK) cells in female mice (Figure 3B–C).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 3B-C.

claim: Treg depletion in female mice partly restores the pro-inflammatory microglial response to CSF1.
source: We conclude that Treg depletion partly restores the pro-inflammatory microglial response to CSF1 in female mice.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from RNA sequencing data of microglia from Treg-depleted female mice.

claim: Female microglia in Treg-depleted mice expressed many of the male-specific CSF1 induced genes, including genes involved in immune activation and recruitment (Clec7a, Il1rn, Ccl3, Ccl4, and Ctsb).
source: We found that female microglia expressed many of the male-specific CSF1 induced genes, including genes involved in immune activation and recruitment (Clec7a, Il1rn, Ccl3, Ccl4, and Ctsb; Figure 3E–F).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA sequencing data shown in Figure 3E-F.

claim: Treg depletion in FoxP3DTR female mice led to a 33% increase in mechanical hypersensitivity compared to wild-type females.
source: Compared to wild-type (WT) females, Treg depletion in females led to a 33% increase in mechanical hypersensitivity (Figure 3H–I; summarizes D3 timepoint from Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral testing data shown in Figure 3H-I.

claim: The effect of Treg depletion on mechanical hypersensitivity in female mice was phenocopied in Rag1−/− mice, which lack T- and B-cells from birth but retain innate lymphocytes, such as NK cells.
source: This effect was phenocopied in Rag1−/−, which lack T- and B-cells from birth but retain innate lymphocytes, such as NK cells (Figure 3J) and the findings are reminiscent of those reported in Rag1−/− female after peripheral nerve injury (Sorge et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral testing data shown in Figure 3J and citation to Sorge et al., 2015.

claim: Depleting Tregs in males did not alter their mechanical hypersensitivity.
source: Of note, depleting Tregs in males did not alter their mechanical hypersensitivity (Figure 3—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral testing data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1G.

claim: Acute antibody blockade of CD4+ T-cells phenocopied the increase in mechanical hypersensitivity seen with Treg depletion in female mice.
source: Acute antibody blockade of CD4+ T-cells, which include both suppressive (Tregs) and inflammatory subsets (Th1/Th2), also phenocopied this increase in mechanical hypersensitivity (Figure 3K; Figure 3—figure supplement 1H-I).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral testing data shown in Figure 3K and Figure 3—figure supplement 1H-I.

claim: The sex difference in CSF1-mediated pain reflects a suppressive effect of Tregs on the CSF1-mediated immune activation in female mice, rather than a direct pain-mediating effect of T-cells on dorsal horn pain circuitry.
source: Taken together, we demonstrate that this difference reflects a suppressive effect of Tregs on the CSF1-mediated immune activation in female mice, rather than a direct pain-mediating effect of T-cells on dorsal horn pain circuitry.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data on Treg depletion and CD4+ T-cell blockade.

claim: One function of CSF1-stimulated myeloid cells is to recruit other immune cells that in turn release cytokines and chemokines to impact microglial function.
source: These results are consistent with a model in which one function of CSF1-stimulated myeloid cells is to recruit other immune cells that in turn release cytokines and chemokines to impact microglial function.
evidence: This is a model proposed based on the observed expansion of lymphocytes in the meninges after CSF1 treatment.

claim: In males, the balance of immune response to CSF1 tips toward pro-inflammatory signaling.
source: However, the nature of this immune response is strikingly sex-specific. In males, the balance tips toward pro-inflammatory signaling.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the transcriptomic and behavioral data showing increased inflammatory activation in males.

claim: In females, Tregs suppress inflammatory activation and limit mechanical hypersensitivity development, despite expansion of the myeloid and lymphoid compartments.
source: In females, Tregs suppress inflammatory activation and limit mechanical hypersensitivity development, despite expansion of the myeloid and lymphoid compartments.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the Treg depletion experiments and transcriptomic data.

claim: Female microglia are competent to contribute to pain hypersensitivity.
source: As intrathecal CSF1 induces mechanical hypersensitivity in Treg-depleted female mice, we concur that female microglia are indeed competent to contribute to pain hypersensitivity (Yi et al., 2021; Sorge et al., 2015).
evidence: This conclusion is supported by the experimental data from Treg-depleted female mice and citations to Yi et al., 2021 and Sorge et al., 2015.

claim: CSF1-mediated cross-talk between spinal cord microglia and lymphocytes can either amplify or suppress pain phenotypes.
source: However, our results demonstrate that CSF1-mediated cross-talk between spinal cord microglia and lymphocytes can either amplify or suppress pain phenotypes.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the sex-specific differences in immune responses and pain outcomes.

claim: Lymphocytes were rarely detected in the spinal cord, even after nerve injury.
source: Importantly, in contrast with a previous report (Costigan et al., 2009), we rarely detected lymphocytes, including T-cells, in the spinal cord, even after nerve injury (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2 and contrasts with a citation to Costigan et al., 2009.

claim: Immune cells markedly expand within the spinal cord meninges, even when absent from the parenchyma.
source: However, we found that immune cells markedly expand within the spinal cord meninges, even when absent from the parenchyma.
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data of meningeal immune cells.

claim: Lymphocytes act primarily via secreted cytokines.
source: As lymphocytes act primarily via secreted cytokines, we suggest that release of meningeal-derived cytokines impacts microglial function as well as directly impacts nociceptors (Liu et al., 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge about lymphocyte function, supported by a citation to Liu et al., 2014.

claim: Release of meningeal-derived cytokines impacts microglial function and directly impacts nociceptors.
source: As lymphocytes act primarily via secreted cytokines, we suggest that release of meningeal-derived cytokines impacts microglial function as well as directly impacts nociceptors (Liu et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism based on the observed meningeal immune cell expansion and citation to Liu et al., 2014.

claim: A female-specific increase in meningeal NK cells was detected in response to CSF1.
source: Although our report focuses on the contribution of Tregs, we also detected a female-specific increase in meningeal NK cells in response to CSF1.
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data of meningeal immune cells.

claim: NK cells are classically associated with pro-inflammatory responses.
source: NK cells are classically associated with pro-inflammatory responses, however, recent studies highlight their more diverse functions.
evidence: This is established knowledge about NK cell function.

claim: Recent studies highlight diverse functions of NK cells, including instruction of anti-inflammatory astrocytes from meningeal NK cells.
source: These include instruction of anti-inflammatory astrocytes from meningeal NK cells (Sanmarco et al., 2021), beneficial effects after peripheral nerve injury (Davies et al., 2019), and a negative correlation between NK cells in the cerebrospinal fluid and mechanical pain sensitivity in chronic neuropathic pain patients (Lassen et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Sanmarco et al., 2021, Davies et al., 2019, and Lassen et al., 2021.

claim: NK cells have beneficial effects after peripheral nerve injury.
source: These include instruction of anti-inflammatory astrocytes from meningeal NK cells (Sanmarco et al., 2021), beneficial effects after peripheral nerve injury (Davies et al., 2019), and a negative correlation between NK cells in the cerebrospinal fluid and mechanical pain sensitivity in chronic neuropathic pain patients (Lassen et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Davies et al., 2019.

claim: There is a negative correlation between NK cells in the cerebrospinal fluid and mechanical pain sensitivity in chronic neuropathic pain patients.
source: These include instruction of anti-inflammatory astrocytes from meningeal NK cells (Sanmarco et al., 2021), beneficial effects after peripheral nerve injury (Davies et al., 2019), and a negative correlation between NK cells in the cerebrospinal fluid and mechanical pain sensitivity in chronic neuropathic pain patients (Lassen et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Lassen et al., 2021.

claim: In the setting of injury, inflammatory signaling at multiple access points (e.g., injury site, nerve, and DRG) activates nociceptive circuits.
source: In the setting of injury, inflammatory signaling at multiple access points (e.g., injury site, nerve, and DRG) activates nociceptive circuits (Yu et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Yu et al., 2020.

claim: Modulating the meninges is a potential therapeutic avenue for neuropathic pain management.
source: However, our finding that intrathecal activation of myeloid cells is sufficient to activate meningeal immunity raises the possibility that modulating the meninges is a potential therapeutic avenue of neuropathic pain management, by suppressing meningeal Treg expansion-mediated microglial activation or by the release of intrathecal immune modulators that override peripheral inflammatory cues.
evidence: This is a speculative therapeutic implication drawn from the findings.

claim: Human genetic analyses and other studies indicate a contribution of Tregs and their dominant cytokines in neuropathic and inflammatory pain models.
source: Given that human genetic analyses and other studies indicate a contribution of Tregs and their dominant cytokines in neuropathic and inflammatory pain models (Davoli-Ferreira et al., 2020; Fischer et al., 2019; Milligan et al., 2006; Eijkelkamp et al., 2016; Echeverry et al., 2009; Kringel et al., 2018), further investigations of Treg localization and impact on microglia will be relevant to understanding the generation and conceivably the treatment of nerve-injury-induced chronic pain.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple studies: Davoli-Ferreira et al., 2020; Fischer et al., 2019; Milligan et al., 2006; Eijkelkamp et al., 2016; Echeverry et al., 2009; Kringel et al., 2018.

claim: In the spinal cord, parenchymal microglia are the only cells expressing CSF1 receptor (CSF1R).
source: CSF1 is de novo expressed in injured sensory neurons (Guan et al., 2016), and in the spinal cord, parenchymal microglia are the only cells expressing CSF1 receptor (CSF1R).
evidence: This is stated as a known fact, supported by citation to Guan et al., 2016.

claim: CSF1 is de novo expressed in injured sensory neurons.
source: CSF1 is de novo expressed in injured sensory neurons (Guan et al., 2016), and in the spinal cord, parenchymal microglia are the only cells expressing CSF1 receptor (CSF1R).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Guan et al., 2016.
